strategies.summary: Implement a custom CUDA scaled-dot-product attention path that fuses QK^T, scaling, row-wise softmax, and AV into a tiled kernel to reduce global-memory traffic and avoid materializing the full attention matrix.
implementation_hints: Add a CUDA entrypoint in cuda_cpp/cuda_cu and switch the forward call site to it while keeping ModelNew I/O unchanged.

Use block tiling over sequence dimensions and head/value tiles so each CTA computes partial score tiles, applies scaling immediately, performs online or two-pass row-wise softmax, and accumulates output against V.
Keep mask/softmax axis semantics identical to torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention even if the current benchmark path is unmasked.
Accumulate reductions in higher precision than storage where practical to protect softmax stability for float32 inputs and future mixed-precision reuse.
strategies.expected_gain: High, especially from eliminating the explicit [B,H,L,L] score tensor and reducing DRAM bandwidth pressure on long sequence length 512.
risk_notes: Preserve Q/K/V order, scaling, mask behavior, and softmax axis exactly.
Numerical drift can appear if using aggressive fusion or fast-math intrinsics around exp/reduction.
Register/shared-memory pressure may reduce occupancy if tile sizes are chosen too aggressively.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Highest upside if implemented well: full fused SDPA removes the O(L^2) score materialization and directly targets the main bottleneck. Risk is real due to softmax/mask semantics and register/shared-memory pressure, but the potential benchmark value is large enough to justify it.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Full FlashAttention-style fused kernel eliminating the O(N^2) score tensor is the highest-value approach for L=512, D=1024. Tiled QK^T + online softmax + AV accumulation in one kernel dramatically cuts DRAM traffic. Well-scoped to the right anchors. Risk is implementation complexity and register/smem pressure at D=1024, but the expected gain is the highest of any strategy here.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Implementing a fused FlashAttention-style kernel is the optimal approach for scaled dot-product attention, significantly reducing memory bandwidth by avoiding the materialization of the O(N^2) attention matrix.

strategies.summary: Implement FlashAttention-style tiling with online softmax to fuse QK^T, softmax, and output computation.
implementation_hints: Tile the sequence length dimension (e.g., Br=16, Bc=16) to avoid materializing the full N x N attention matrix.
Maintain running maximums and sums for the online softmax computation.
Scale the QK^T dot products by 1/sqrt(head_dim) before updating the softmax statistics.
strategies.expected_gain: Significant reduction in global memory traffic and memory footprint, avoiding O(N^2) memory complexity.
risk_notes: Numerical stability of online softmax requires careful implementation.
High register pressure due to large head_dim (1024).

review_notes.openai-compatible: Conceptually strong and aligned with the right optimization pattern, but risk-adjusted value is slightly lower than strategy_01 because the FlashAttention-style description is high level and the very large head_dim=1024 makes implementation pressure much higher.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Essentially the same FlashAttention tiling approach as strategy_01 but from a different model. Br=16, Bc=16 tile sizes are conservative and safe for D=1024. Online softmax with running max/sum is the correct algorithm. The head_dim=1024 register pressure concern is real and worth flagging, but this is the right architectural direction. Scores equally high.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: FlashAttention with online softmax is the standard state-of-the-art optimization for this operation. Tiling the sequence length is essential.

strategies.summary: Optimize the CUDA kernel around memory hierarchy: stage K/V tiles in shared memory, stream Q fragments through registers, and use warp-level reductions for the softmax statistics and output accumulation.
implementation_hints: Treat the head dimension 1024 as a reduction axis amenable to vectorized loads and warp-partitioned dot products, with cooperative loading into shared memory for K/V tiles.
Use warp shuffles or cooperative reductions for per-row max and sum computations to minimize shared-memory synchronization overhead.
Consider double-buffered tile staging so global-memory fetch of the next K/V tile overlaps with arithmetic on the current tile.
Tune tile sizes for the benchmark’s L=512, D=1024 regime rather than for full generality first.
strategies.expected_gain: Medium to high; improves arithmetic intensity and reduces synchronization and memory latency in the fused kernel.
risk_notes: Shared-memory bank conflicts and register pressure can offset gains if tile shapes are poorly chosen.
Vectorization requires alignment and contiguous last-dimension assumptions.
Backend flags include --use_fast_math; verify it does not destabilize the softmax reduction path beyond tolerance.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Good kernel-level guidance once a fused kernel exists. Shared-memory staging, warp reductions, and double-buffering are relevant for this workload, though they are secondary tuning steps rather than a complete strategy on their own. Solid but implementation-sensitive.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Memory hierarchy optimization: shared memory staging for K/V, register streaming for Q, warp-level reductions, double-buffering. These are important micro-optimizations that complement the tiling strategies. Particularly relevant for D=1024 where vectorized loads and warp shuffles for softmax stats can meaningfully reduce latency. Good risk-adjusted value as an enhancement layer on top of strategy_01/02.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Excellent low-level implementation details for the fused kernel. Using warp-level reductions and staging tiles in shared memory are critical for achieving high performance.

strategies.summary: Add shape/dtype/layout-aware dispatch so the custom CUDA kernel is only used on the dominant benchmark case, with fallback to the native PyTorch path for unsupported layouts or edge cases.
implementation_hints: In user_helpers, centralize checks for device, dtype, dimensionality, contiguity/stride assumptions, and sequence/head dimensions before calling the extension.
Restrict the fast path initially to CUDA float32 tensors matching the benchmark’s dense non-broadcasted Q/K/V shape profile; otherwise preserve the existing functional call.
Expose minimal metadata validation in the C++ entrypoint as a second line of defense before launching CUDA.
Keep the forward-site swap small and reversible: choose extension path only when all semantic and layout preconditions hold.
strategies.expected_gain: Medium overall; avoids slowdown/regressions from forcing a custom kernel onto unsupported or poorly aligned cases, while preserving benchmark wins on the hot path.
risk_notes: Overly strict guards can reduce fast-path hit rate.
Stride/layout assumptions must be audited carefully because benchmark tensors may be contiguous but future variants may not be.
Fallback must remain semantically identical to avoid silent behavior changes.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Very strong risk-adjusted value. Guarded dispatch and fallback logic are highly useful when introducing a custom CUDA path for attention, helping preserve semantics and avoid regressions on unsupported layouts or dtypes. Low cost, high practical value.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Dispatch/guard layer strategy. Useful for robustness and avoiding regressions but provides no direct speedup on its own. Valuable as a companion to strategies 01/02/03 to protect correctness. Standalone score is limited since it adds overhead without kernel improvement. Worth implementing alongside a fast-path kernel.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Adding dispatch guards is good engineering practice for safety, but does not provide direct performance gains for the kernel itself.

strategies.summary: Use shared memory caching with block-level matrix multiplication to handle the large head dimension (1024).
implementation_hints: Since head_dim=1024 is large, a full sequence block might exceed shared memory capacity.
Implement an inner loop over the head_dim to compute QK^T dot products in chunks, loading sub-tiles of Q and K into shared memory.
Similarly, loop over head_dim when computing the final attention output with V.
strategies.expected_gain: Allows the kernel to run within shared memory limits while maximizing data reuse.
risk_notes: Complex synchronization and indexing logic.
Potential shared memory bank conflicts if padding is not applied.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Reasonable supporting tactic for handling the large head dimension within shared-memory limits. Useful as an implementation detail, but broad and somewhat generic; by itself it does not guarantee strong gains beyond what a better overall fused design would already require.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Addresses the critical constraint that D=1024 is too large to fit full tiles in shared memory. Chunked inner-loop over head_dim for QK^T and AV is the correct approach for this problem size. Practical and necessary for any custom kernel targeting this benchmark. Slightly lower score than strategy_01/02 because it's a component technique rather than a complete solution.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Addressing the large head dimension (1024) is a crucial practical consideration, as it will likely require inner-loop tiling to fit within shared memory limits.

strategies.summary: Utilize warp-level primitives for fast softmax reductions.
implementation_hints: Use `__shfl_down_sync` to perform fast parallel reductions (max and sum) across threads within a warp.
Assign one warp per sequence row (or multiple rows if Br > warps_per_block) to compute the softmax statistics efficiently without shared memory bottlenecks.
strategies.expected_gain: Lower latency for the reduction steps of the online softmax compared to shared memory reductions.
risk_notes: Requires careful handling of thread indexing and warp divergence.
Assumes block dimensions are multiples of the warp size (32).

review_notes.openai-compatible: Warp-level softmax reductions are a sensible micro-optimization, but the total value is modest unless integrated carefully into a larger fused kernel. Helpful, though not a primary strategy and somewhat sensitive to row/tile mapping.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Warp-level primitives (__shfl_down_sync) for softmax max/sum reductions are a well-established optimization that reduces shared memory pressure and synchronization overhead. One warp per row is a natural fit for L=512 rows. Clean, targeted, and composable with other strategies. Risk is low given standard CUDA warp primitives.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Using warp-level primitives (`__shfl_down_sync`) for the online softmax reductions is highly recommended to minimize latency and shared memory synchronization overhead.

strategies.summary: Optimize global memory bandwidth using vectorized loads and stores.
implementation_hints: Cast pointers to `float4` to load and store 128 bits per thread.
Ensure that the inner dimensions (head_dim=1024) are accessed contiguously by threads in a warp to achieve fully coalesced memory transactions.
strategies.expected_gain: Higher global memory throughput, reducing the memory bound nature of the attention computation.
risk_notes: Alignment issues if tensor pointers or dimensions are not multiples of 4 (though 1024 is safe).
Increases register usage per thread.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Vectorized memory ops can improve throughput given aligned contiguous inner dimensions, but this is an incremental optimization and can raise register pressure. Worth considering after the main fused algorithm is working, not as a leading optimization bet.
review_notes.claude-compatible: float4 vectorized loads for D=1024 (divisible by 4) is straightforward and effective for improving memory throughput. Coalesced access along the head dimension is achievable with correct thread layout. Low risk given alignment guarantees. Incremental but reliable gain, especially for the memory-bound portions of the kernel.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Vectorized memory accesses (e.g., `float4`) are a standard and highly effective way to maximize global memory bandwidth utilization.

review_notes.openai-compatible: Moderate, safer optimization: fusing scale+softmax can help bandwidth, but it still leaves both matmuls untouched, so total gain may be limited if GEMMs dominate. Useful fallback if full fusion is too risky, but not the best primary bet.
review_notes.claude-compatible: Partial fusion: keeps matmuls in PyTorch but fuses scale+softmax into a custom kernel. Pragmatic and lower-risk than full FlashAttention. However, the intermediate score tensor is still materialized, so memory savings are partial. 512 threads/block for 512-wide rows is a clean fit. Moderate gain, moderate risk — a reasonable fallback if full fusion is too complex.
review_notes.gemini-compatible: Partial fusion (keeping matmuls separate and only fusing scale+softmax) leaves a lot of performance on the table compared to full FlashAttention, as it still materializes the O(N^2) intermediate tensor.

import torch
import torch.nn as nn
import hashlib
from torch.utils.cpp_extension import load_inline

_STARK_EXTENSION = None

def _stark_strip_anchor_markers(source: str) -> str:
    cleaned_lines = []
    for line in source.splitlines():
        stripped = line.lstrip()
        if stripped.startswith('# <<<IMPROVE:') or stripped.startswith('# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>'):
            continue
        cleaned_lines.append(line)
    return '\n'.join(cleaned_lines)

def _stark_extension_name() -> str:
    digest = hashlib.sha1((_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CPP_SRC) + _stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CU_SRC)).encode('utf-8')).hexdigest()[:12]
    return f'stark_cuda_l1_p97_{digest}'

def _stark_get_extension():
    global _STARK_EXTENSION
    if _STARK_EXTENSION is None:
        _STARK_EXTENSION = load_inline(
            name=_stark_extension_name(),
            cpp_sources=_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CPP_SRC),
            cuda_sources=_stark_strip_anchor_markers(CUDA_CU_SRC),
            functions=None,
            extra_cflags=['-O3'],
            extra_cuda_cflags=['-O3', '--use_fast_math'],
            with_cuda=True,
            verbose=False,
        )
    return _STARK_EXTENSION

# <<<IMPROVE:user_helpers>>>
# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>

CUDA_CPP_SRC = r"""
# <<<IMPROVE:cuda_cpp>>>
#include <torch/extension.h>

// Add pybind exports for custom CUDA entrypoints here.
PYBIND11_MODULE(TORCH_EXTENSION_NAME, m) {}
# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
"""

CUDA_CU_SRC = r"""
# <<<IMPROVE:cuda_cu>>>
#include <torch/extension.h>
#include <cuda.h>
#include <cuda_runtime.h>

// Add CUDA kernels and exported wrapper functions here.
# <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
"""

class ModelNew(nn.Module):
    def __init__(self):
        super().__init__()
        # <<<IMPROVE:init_body>>>
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>

    def forward(self, Q: torch.Tensor, K: torch.Tensor, V: torch.Tensor) -> torch.Tensor:
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_1>>>
        # Baseline fallback keeps the official PyTorch forward path.
        # After implementing CUDA_CPP_SRC / CUDA_CU_SRC, call _stark_get_extension().your_entrypoint(...).
        out = torch.nn.functional.scaled_dot_product_attention(Q, K, V)
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
        # <<<IMPROVE:forward_stmt_2>>>
        return out
        # <<<END_IMPROVE>>>
